summary:
AGNI (Active-fire Global Normalized Inventory) turns NASA's two incompatible active-fire records into one consistent hotspot history from 2000 to today, and presents it as a burning activity calendar in a free web application. MODIS has observed fires since 2000 but is nearing the end of its life; VIIRS, its successor since 2012, detects much smaller fires, so raw counts jump when the instrument changes and not when fire activity does. Our harmonization model, Harmonic, learns from the 14 years in which both sensors flew together what VIIRS would have recorded wherever MODIS saw fire, and converts the 2000–2011 MODIS record into VIIRS-equivalent detections. On held-out data it reproduces real VIIRS monthly totals with an R² of 0.996 and a typical error of 3%. In the web application a user selects a region or draws an area on the map and sees, within seconds, how the current month compares with the historical median, how it ranks against every year on record, which months and years burned most, and can download the detections as a CSV file. AGNI gives emergency managers, land managers and scientists a fire baseline that stays usable after MODIS retires, at no running cost.

Github Repo - https://github.com/its-thakshila/AGNI
details:
1. The problem we address

Emergency managers judge a fire season by comparing it with the past: is this month normal for this area, or dangerous? That comparison needs a long and consistent history, and the raw satellite record is not consistent.

  • MODIS (Terra and Aqua) has detected fires at 1 km resolution since 2000 and is approaching the end of its operational life.
  • VIIRS has detected fires at 375 m resolution since 2012. It sees much smaller and cooler fires, and one fire often covers several of its pixels.

A calendar built from raw hotspot counts therefore shows a sharp rise in 2012 that is caused by the instrument, not by fire. A manager reading it would conclude that fire activity had multiplied. The challenge asks for a record in which the sensor of origin no longer matters, and that is what AGNI provides.

2. What AGNI does

AGNI has two parts, matching the two parts of the challenge.

A harmonized hotspot record. Every detection from 2000 to today is expressed in one unit, the VIIRS S-NPP equivalent detection:

  • 2000 to 2011: MODIS detections converted by our model, Harmonic.
  • 2012 to today: VIIRS S-NPP detections as observed.
  • Any day on which VIIRS has no data in FIRMS: filled by Harmonic from that day's MODIS detections, and labelled as such.

A web application for decisions. The user picks a region or draws an area on the map, and the application answers in plain language:

  • Headline: the number of detections this month, the percentage above or below usual, and the month's rank among all years (for example "1st of 26 years").
  • Burn calendar: one row per year and one column per month from 2000 to today. It can show the amount of fire, or each month against its own historical median (red above, blue below).
  • Month view: detections day by day with the model's uncertainty shaded, and the same month in every year next to the usual level.
  • Trends: harmonized annual totals, the busiest month and year, and the typical seasonal curve against the current year.
  • Download: the detections for the selected area and period as a CSV file.

3. How it works

  1. Ingest. MODIS Collection 6.1 and VIIRS S-NPP 375 m active-fire hotspots are downloaded from NASA FIRMS.
  2. Common grid. Detections are grouped into 0.1° cells by local fire-day and by day or night pass. A fire-day runs from 6 am to 6 am local solar time, so a night overpass belongs to the evening it follows.
  3. Features. For each cell, the model receives what MODIS saw: detection counts, fire radiative power, brightness temperatures, confidence, the true pixel size (scan and track), Terra and Aqua kept separately, the eight neighbouring cells, and the days before and after. Cells next to a MODIS detection are included, so the model can place fires that MODIS missed but VIIRS would detect.
  4. Model. Harmonic is a gradient-boosted tree model (XGBoost) trained on the 2012–2025 overlap, about 4.5 million cell-days, to predict the VIIRS S-NPP detection count. A second model covers the period before Aqua's launch in 2002, when only Terra was flying.
  5. Correction. A calibrated weight accounts for small fires far from any MODIS detection, which the model cannot place, so that regional totals remain unbiased.
  6. Serve. Results are stored as Parquet files. The browser reads only the parts each query needs, so any area and date range is answered without a server.
  7. Update. An automated job checks FIRMS every three hours and adds new fire-days.

4. Validation

We tested Harmonic on data it had never seen. Whole weeks were held out in a 4-fold grouped cross-validation over 2012–2025; the model predicted them from MODIS alone, and we compared the result with what VIIRS actually recorded. The table compares Harmonic with the usual simple approach, a fixed MODIS-to-VIIRS ratio.

Total bias is below 0.3%. The Terra-only model used for 2000–2002 reaches a monthly R² of 0.993 with a typical error of 4.9%, against 10.6% for a fixed ratio.

5. Benefits

  • Emergency managers see abnormal months early and can place crews and warnings accordingly.
  • Continuity: 25 years of MODIS history stay comparable with VIIRS after Terra and Aqua are retired.
  • Scientists and land managers get one consistent series for trend, climate and land-use studies.
  • Accessibility: plain-language headlines, colour ramps chosen to be readable with colour-vision deficiency, built-in "How to read" help and notes on the data.
  • Cost: the whole system runs on free tiers with no always-on server, so an agency with no IT budget can host it.

6. Limitations

  • Values before 2012 are model estimates. They are reliable as monthly and regional totals, not as exact fire locations.
  • The method assumes the MODIS-to-VIIRS relationship learned in 2012–2025 also held in 2000–2011.
  • Cloud and smoke hide fires from both sensors, and this is not corrected.
  • The overpass times of Terra and Aqua have drifted in recent years, which slowly changes what MODIS observes.
  • The prototype covers Australia. Other regions require their own data build and model check.

7. What comes next

  • More regions, then global coverage.
  • Alerts by email or SMS when a selected area rises above its normal level.
  • Land-cover inputs and an orbit-drift correction in the model.
  • Pilots with fire and disaster-management agencies.

8. Tools and technology

  • Model and pipeline: Python, pandas, NumPy, XGBoost, scikit-learn, Parquet.
  • Web application: TypeScript, Vite, MapLibre GL, hyparquet.
  • Infrastructure: GitHub Pages, GitHub Actions, Cloudflare R2 and a Cloudflare Worker
